paragraphs: Collecting every possible input for a prediction can be expensive or impractical. This paper studies how a model can choose which information to obtain next for an individual case. Its starting point is that useful features can differ between cases, so a single fixed feature ranking may allocate resources poorly.

The proposed framework uses local explanations to produce rankings of feature importance for individual examples. It then turns acquisition into a prediction problem: a policy network learns which feature should come next from these rankings. The network uses a decision transformer architecture, allowing the acquisition process to proceed as a sequence of choices guided by predictive importance.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report better predictive accuracy and acquisition efficiency than existing state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects explanations of model behavior with decisions about collecting data. In the evaluated settings, those explanations provide useful supervision for acquiring informative features sequentially, addressing applications where the cost of obtaining inputs matters alongside prediction quality.
icml-2025-active-feature-acquisition-via.tldr: An acquisition policy learns from instance-specific explanations to select useful features sequentially, improving accuracy and acquisition efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines how language models attend to graph information expressed through natural language. Graph tasks depend on relationships between nodes, making it important to distinguish recognizing graph-related text from representing the connections themselves. The authors investigate that distinction through an empirical study of attention behavior.

Their experiments find that language models can recognize graph data and capture interactions between text and nodes, yet struggle with relationships between nodes. They attribute this difficulty to architectural constraints and observe attention patterns that do not match the graph's desired structural relationships. The findings therefore identify a gap between processing a graph's description and adapting attention to its topology.

The study also examines connectivity choices. In the investigated scenarios, unrestricted attention and the fixed connections used by graph neural networks each have limitations. Intermediate attention windows improve language-model training performance and can transition to fully connected windows at inference. This suggests that controlling connectivity during training can help models process graph structure without requiring the same restriction when they are used.
icml-2025-attention-mechanisms-perspecti.tldr: An empirical study identifies shortcomings in language-model attention over graphs and finds benefits from intermediate attention windows during training.

paragraphs: Prompt caching speeds up processing when an API can reuse work from an earlier prompt. This paper investigates a privacy consequence of that optimization: response speed can depend on whether a prompt is already cached. If users share a cache, timing may reveal information about prompts submitted by someone else.

The authors develop statistical audits that use these timing differences to detect caching behavior in real language-model APIs. They report detecting cache sharing across users at seven providers, including OpenAI. This establishes a potential route for privacy leakage through an observable feature of the service, even when the service does not directly disclose another user's prompt.

The audits also explore what timing can reveal about model design. The authors find evidence that OpenAI's embedding model uses a decoder-only Transformer architecture, information they describe as previously undisclosed. These findings make caching transparency consequential for both user privacy and architectural confidentiality. The privacy conclusion concerns potential leakage from the detected sharing behavior, rather than a claim that every cached prompt was recovered.
icml-2025-auditing-prompt-caching-in-lan.tldr: Statistical timing audits detect shared prompt caches across seven API providers, exposing potential privacy leakage and clues about model architecture.

paragraphs: Updating a fact in a multimodal model raises two linked questions: how broadly should the correction apply, and which other knowledge should remain unaffected? The paper describes this as a trade-off between generality and locality. Different facts have different ranges of influence, making a uniform approach to editing problematic.

The authors introduce OKEDIT, a dataset designed to evaluate this balance, and propose BalancEdit to adapt an edit's scope to the fact being changed. The method generates positive and negative examples for each fact to determine that scope. It incorporates the resulting information into the model's latent space through a discrete codebook of localized edits, leaving the underlying model weights unchanged.

The reported results show effective editing with minimal trade-offs between generality and locality. The approach makes the intended reach of a correction an explicit part of the editing process. Its contribution combines a benchmark for measuring that behavior with a method designed to preserve useful generalization while limiting effects beyond the relevant fact.
icml-2025-balancedit-dynamically-balanci.tldr: BalancEdit uses fact-specific examples and localized latent edits to balance how broadly multimodal knowledge updates apply.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning data can appear harmless while still weakening a language model's safety behavior. This paper investigates whether some benign examples contribute disproportionately to that degradation. Its red-teaming objective is to identify those examples and test how strongly they can affect alignment when used as the fine-tuning data.

The authors frame sample selection as an outlier-detection problem and introduce Self-Inf-N to identify and extract unusual examples from benign datasets. They report that fine-tuning on just 100 selected outliers severely compromises safety alignment. The result makes the composition of a benign dataset important: its apparent harmlessness does not establish that adaptation on it will preserve safety.

Experiments across seven mainstream language models show high transferability across architectures and effectiveness in practical scenarios. The authors also report that most existing mitigation strategies they examine fail against the attack. These findings identify a specific weakness in fine-tuning safeguards and motivate protections that account for the effects of selected training examples, beyond whether their content is overtly harmful.
icml-2025-benign-samples-matter-fine-tun.tldr: Fine-tuning on 100 carefully selected benign outliers severely weakens safety alignment in the reported language-model experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many observations are needed to distinguish between two possible probabilistic models. Its main setting is a softmax model: a vector goes in, and an output is sampled from a distribution determined by that input. This abstracts a distributional component used in language-model attention into a mathematical testing problem.

The unknown model is assumed to be one of two specified candidates. The authors show an asymptotic query-complexity upper bound of O(ε⁻²), where ε measures a particular distance between their parameters. The inverse-square dependence describes how the bound grows as candidate models become closer under that distance. It is an upper bound on the required observations, rather than a stated exact count for every pair.

The authors then connect this setup to leverage-score models, which also return samples from input-dependent distributions and are useful in linear algebra and graph algorithms. They obtain similar testing results there. The contribution provides a shared perspective on identifying two kinds of probabilistic models through queries, under the explicit two-candidate assumption.
icml-2025-binary-hypothesis-testing-for-.tldr: The paper bounds the queries needed to distinguish two candidate softmax models and obtains analogous results for leverage-score models.

paragraphs: Proteins move, but many graph-based models describe them using only static structural information. This paper asks how motion information from molecular dynamics trajectories can improve those representations. The central idea is to combine a protein's structural description with correlations observed in its changing behavior.

The proposed graph representation includes both static information and dynamic correlations. A relational graph neural network processes this heterogeneous representation, allowing the model to use the different kinds of relationships together. This gives dynamic observations an explicit place in the graph representation used for prediction, addressing the limited use of trajectories in existing computational approaches.

The authors report significant improvements over structure-based approaches on atomic adaptability prediction, binding site detection, and binding affinity prediction. Gains across these three tasks support the claim that static and dynamic information supply complementary signals about protein-ligand interactions. The work points to potential uses in drug design and structural biology by showing that incorporating motion can improve the protein representations underlying these predictions.
icml-2025-boosting-protein-graph-represe.tldr: Combining protein structure with dynamic correlations improves graph-model predictions across three protein-related tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when the learner cannot inspect complete feature vectors directly. Instead, each observation measures one chosen feature of one chosen item and includes noise. The goal is to recover two unknown groups while making as few observations as possible, even when many features are available.

The setting assumes that every item within a group has the same underlying feature vector. The algorithm exploits this structure by searching for a feature useful for separating the groups. It uses Sequential Halving as part of that search and chooses observations adaptively, so its measurement decisions can respond to the information obtained so far.

The authors establish accurate recovery with probability at least 1−δ and give an upper bound on the observation budget. They also derive a lower bound that depends on the particular instance and matches the achievable requirements in some relevant cases. Together, these results characterize both a successful strategy and portions of its efficiency limits under the stated two-group model.
icml-2025-clustering-items-through-bandi.tldr: An adaptive algorithm finds a useful feature for recovering two groups from noisy measurements, with probability guarantees and observation-budget bounds.

paragraphs: Graph anomaly detectors commonly look for unusual connections or attributes. CurvGAD adds a geometric perspective by treating irregular edge curvature as another source of anomalies. The motivation is that reconstruction methods focused on structure and attributes can overlook outliers expressed through the graph's geometry.

The method separates reconstruction into two parallel paths. One reconstructs edge curvatures using a mixed-curvature Riemannian encoder and a Gaussian-kernel decoder. The other reconstructs structure and attributes after regularizing curvature through discrete Ollivier-Ricci flow. This separation is intended to distinguish geometric irregularities from anomalies in connections or attributes, improving the interpretation of what makes something unusual.

Experiments cover ten real-world datasets, including both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The authors report improvements of up to 6.5% over state-of-the-art graph anomaly detection methods. The result supports curvature as a useful additional signal in the evaluated settings. Beyond improving detection, the framework refines anomaly categories by explicitly identifying curvature-driven behavior alongside the structural and attribute irregularities already considered.
icml-2025-curvgad-leveraging-curvature-f.tldr: CurvGAD separates geometric anomalies from structural and attribute anomalies, reporting gains of up to 6.5% across ten graph datasets.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models can require substantial storage and memory because they contain multiple sets of expert weights. D²-MoE compresses these weights by separating what experts share from what makes each expert different. This organization allows the method to target redundancy without treating every expert as an unrelated collection of parameters.

First, the method uses Fisher information to merge shared components into a base weight. Each expert's remaining difference becomes a delta weight, which is compressed through singular value decomposition using its low-rank properties. A further structured-pruning step reduces the base weights, combining static and dynamic redundancy analysis while retaining input adaptivity.

The procedure requires no additional training. In experiments on Mixtral, Phi-3.5, DeepSeek, and Qwen2 MoE models, the authors report performance gains exceeding 13% over other compressors at compression rates of 40–60%. These comparisons concern the quality retained under compression. The contribution is a coordinated way to compress both shared and expert-specific components while preserving their distinct roles.
icml-2025-delta-decompression-for-moe-ba.tldr: D²-MoE compresses shared expert weights and individual differences without additional training, outperforming other compressors in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Observations of a physical system mix its underlying dynamics with effects specific to its environment. This paper aims to recover the common law across environments described by ordinary differential equations. It considers changes that alter entire functional forms, extending beyond changes to coefficients in an otherwise fixed equation.

The proposed method, Disentanglement of Invariant Functions, uses a causal graph and an encoder-decoder hypernetwork to separate shared dynamics from environmental effects. An information-based principle enforces independence between the extracted invariant functions and the environments, providing the basis for the paper's discovery guarantee. The pendulum example illustrates the target: recover natural motion from observations that also include damping or external power.

Comparisons with meta-learning and invariant-learning methods across three differential-equation systems support the approach's effectiveness and efficiency. Symbolic regression results further show its ability to express recovered intrinsic laws. The contribution concerns isolating the common dynamics underlying several environments, so that changes in surrounding mechanisms do not become confused with the system's invariant behavior.
icml-2025-discovering-physics-laws-of-dy.tldr: DIF separates shared physical dynamics from environment-specific effects, recovering invariant laws across systems with changing functional forms.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning trains a language model on input-output examples, but its generative objective does not explicitly use negative answers. This paper explores a discriminative alternative that learns to favor positive answers while suppressing potentially negative ones. It seeks to address limitations commonly handled through a later preference-optimization stage.

Discriminative Fine-Tuning models the likelihood of an answer relative to the possible outputs for an input. This shifts the training emphasis toward distinguishing answers at the data level rather than relying on token prediction alone. The authors develop a probabilistic framework for that objective and efficient algorithms for optimizing it, reducing dependence on human preference labels or a strong reward model.

The reported experiments show better performance than supervised fine-tuning and results comparable to, or better than, supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization. The findings support discriminative learning as a useful route for adapting generative models. Its practical significance is that answer discrimination can be built into fine-tuning itself, mitigating the additional data-collection or reward-model burden associated with preference optimization.
icml-2025-discriminative-finetuning-of-g.tldr: Discriminative Fine-Tuning improves answer selection without human preference data or reward models, matching or exceeding the reported two-stage alternatives.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers behavior from a teacher model to a student by matching their output scores. This paper examines a weakness of the commonly used KL-divergence objective: its gradients depend on the magnitude of teacher logits, leaving low-probability channels with weaker updates. That imbalance can reduce the transfer of relationships between classes.

The authors add an auxiliary loss based on Kendall's τ, a ranking coefficient. It supplies information about inter-class ordering and rebalances learning toward low-probability channels. They show that the loss is largely invariant to channel scaling and has an objective aligned with KL divergence. It is therefore designed to supplement the existing distillation objective.

Experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and COCO include teacher-student combinations built from convolutional networks and vision transformers. The added ranking loss consistently improves multiple distillation baselines in these evaluations. The contribution is a broadly integrable way to preserve relational information that uneven gradients can otherwise underemphasize, strengthening the information passed from teacher to student.
icml-2025-enhancing-logits-distillation-.tldr: An auxiliary Kendall's τ ranking loss improves distillation by strengthening inter-class information and updates to low-probability channels.

paragraphs: Complex planning requires a language model to manage long reasoning sequences, multiple constraints, and distinct subtasks. Success in mathematical or logical reasoning does not automatically resolve those organizational demands. HyperTree Planning addresses them by giving the planning process an explicit hierarchical outline.

The outline uses a hypertree structure to support flexible divide-and-conquer reasoning. Complicated steps can be broken into smaller parts while constraints and different subtasks remain organized within the overall plan. The authors also introduce an autonomous framework that repeatedly refines and expands these outlines, making the hierarchy an evolving part of planning rather than a single preliminary sketch.

On TravelPlanner, the framework paired with Gemini-1.5-Pro achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and a reported 3.6-fold performance improvement over o1-preview. This result supports the usefulness of hierarchical organization for the evaluated planning task. The contribution links an explicit representation of the plan with an iterative process for developing it, helping the model manage several planning requirements within a coordinated structure.
icml-2025-hypertree-planning-enhancing-l.tldr: HyperTree Planning iteratively develops hierarchical outlines, achieving a reported 3.6-fold improvement over o1-preview on TravelPlanner with Gemini-1.5-Pro.

paragraphs: Complex query answering is intended to test reasoning over knowledge graphs, including questions involving several connections. This paper finds that existing benchmark construction can make such tasks easier than their form suggests. A query that appears to require several reasoning steps may reduce to predicting a single missing link.

The authors report that up to 98% of queries for some benchmark query types can be simplified into easier problems. When state-of-the-art models are evaluated on queries that cannot be reduced this way, performance falls significantly. This means strong aggregate scores on those benchmarks can give an inflated impression of progress on genuinely multi-step reasoning.

The paper introduces harder benchmarks whose queries require reasoning across multiple hops and whose construction better reflects real-world knowledge graphs. A systematic empirical evaluation reveals substantial remaining weaknesses in current methods. The contribution changes what the evaluation demands: it makes successful performance depend more directly on the reasoning capability the task is supposed to measure.
icml-2025-is-complex-query-answering-rea.tldr: Many complex-query benchmarks admit simpler solutions, and new benchmarks requiring multiple hops expose substantial weaknesses in current methods.

paragraphs: Topological data analysis describes the overall shape and higher-order structure of a point cloud. Tools such as persistent homology produce a description of the collection as a whole. Many machine-learning applications, however, need features attached to individual points, creating a gap between global shape information and the form needed for prediction.

This paper introduces topological point features, or TOPF, to bridge that gap. The method uses discrete versions of ideas from algebraic topology and differential geometry to extract features at the node level. Its central contribution is to make information about complex point-cloud structure available as representations associated with individual points.

The authors verify the effectiveness of these features on synthetic and real-world data. They also study robustness under noise and heterogeneous sampling, examining the method when observations are perturbed or unevenly distributed. The work thus connects tools for describing global structure with point-level learning, while investigating how the resulting representations behave under changes in the observed cloud.
icml-2025-point-level-topological-repres.tldr: TOPF turns point-cloud topology into point-level features and evaluates their effectiveness under noise and uneven sampling.

paragraphs: Mathematical benchmarks become less informative when scores approach saturation or problems may have appeared in training data. Putnam-AXIOM addresses both issues with 522 university-level competition problems and a companion set of 100 unseen variants. The variants are created by programmatically changing variables and constants while preserving difficulty.

The variation protocol can generate an unlimited stream of new instances, supporting evaluation that is more resilient to contamination. Among the evaluated models, o1-preview performs best on the original set at 41.9%, but its accuracy falls by 19.6 percentage points on paired variations. All eighteen other models also decline, with ten showing non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.

These gaps suggest memorization may contribute to performance and motivate dynamic evaluation; they do not by themselves establish memorization as the sole explanation. The benchmark also introduces Teacher-Forced Accuracy, a lightweight measure that scores reasoning traces and automates natural-language proof evaluation. Together, varied problems and reasoning-sensitive scoring broaden the assessment beyond correctness of a final boxed answer.
icml-2025-putnam-axiom-a-functional-stat.tldr: Putnam-AXIOM combines difficult competition problems, generated variants, and reasoning-trace scoring, revealing performance drops that suggest memorization.

paragraphs: Image quality assessment asks models to judge visual quality, making perceptual capability central to the task. This paper investigates that capability in vision Mamba, a state-space model architecture whose use in other vision tasks had received more attention. The authors adapt it into QMamba for task-specific, universal, and transferable quality assessment.

A second contribution, StylePrompt, supports adapting a pretrained QMamba model to downstream quality-assessment tasks. It introduces lightweight prompts based on means and variances to guide task-adaptive transfer learning. The authors report better perceptual transfer with lower computational cost than existing prompt-tuning strategies.

Experiments span synthetic and authentic image-quality datasets, as well as evaluations across datasets. The reported results show advantages over Swin Transformer, ViT, and convolutional models in perception and computational cost. The contribution therefore combines an assessment of Mamba's suitability for visual-quality judgments with a lightweight adaptation method, addressing both the quality of those judgments and the cost of transferring them to different tasks.
icml-2025-qmamba-on-first-exploration-of.tldr: QMamba adapts vision Mamba for image quality assessment, while StylePrompt improves perceptual transfer at lower reported computational cost.

paragraphs: rStar-Math investigates how small language models can achieve strong mathematical reasoning without distillation from stronger models. It combines a small model that proposes reasoning steps with a small process reward model that guides Monte Carlo Tree Search at test time. Search gives the system a way to explore reasoning paths before settling on a solution.

Training uses code-augmented synthesis to generate step-by-step verified trajectories through extensive search. A process preference model learns guidance without naïve step-level score annotation. The policy and preference models then improve together through an iterative self-evolution procedure. The reported training spans four rounds and millions of synthesized solutions for 747,000 problems.

On MATH, Qwen2.5-Math-7B improves from 58.8% to 90.0%, exceeding o1-preview by 4.5 percentage points. The system also solves an average of 53.3% of AIME problems, or eight out of fifteen. These results support the paper's claim that small models, combined with learned search guidance and iterative training, can rival or surpass stronger reference models on the evaluated mathematical tasks.
icml-2025-rstar-math-small-llms-can-mast.tldr: rStar-Math combines small models, guided search, and iterative self-training to reach 90.0% on MATH without stronger-model distillation.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct unseen data from measurements that may be corrupted or perturbed. Model-based architectures organize this reconstruction around an iterative procedure, but good reconstruction quality alone does not settle questions about generalization and robustness. This paper studies a training strategy intended to improve those properties together.

SGD jittering injects noise at individual reconstruction iterations during training. The authors theoretically show better generalization than standard mean-squared-error training and greater robustness to average-case attacks. The stated robustness result concerns that attack setting, giving a specific meaning to the theoretical improvement rather than an unrestricted guarantee against every perturbation.

Experiments cover toy denoising, seismic deconvolution, and single-coil MRI reconstruction. Both SGD jittering and its SPGD extension produce cleaner reconstructions for out-of-distribution data and show enhanced resistance to adversarial attacks. These findings connect the theoretical analysis with several reconstruction settings, supporting iteration-wise noise injection as a simple way to improve how model-based architectures handle unfamiliar or perturbed measurements.
icml-2025-sgd-jittering-a-training-strat.tldr: Injecting noise during reconstruction training improves generalization and average-case robustness theoretically, with supporting results across three inverse-problem settings.

paragraphs: Structured pruning reduces a language model by removing components such as channels or attention heads. The challenge is deciding which components matter and limiting the performance lost when they disappear. SlimLLM addresses both decisions with a fast pruning method designed around the structure of the model's submodules.

For channels and attention heads, SlimLLM evaluates importance at the level of the entire component. This accounts for interdependence among its elements instead of relying only on an aggregation of individual element scores. The method also uses layer-based importance ratios to decide how much to prune from each layer, making the allocation depend on layer importance.

After pruning, a simple linear regression strategy adjusts the output matrix to recover performance quickly. The authors report that SlimLLM outperforms other methods and achieves state-of-the-art results on LLaMA benchmarks. The approach combines component-level assessment, layer-specific pruning allocation, and output recovery, showing how several targeted choices can work together to preserve quality while reducing model parameters.
icml-2025-slimllm-accurate-structured-pr.tldr: SlimLLM combines whole-component importance scoring, layer-specific pruning, and linear-regression recovery to improve structured pruning on LLaMA benchmarks.

paragraphs: Test-time training adapts a model's weights using information available for the current test instance. This paper studies that idea for in-context learning, where a prompt contains demonstrations of the target task. The proposed setup trains the transformer on those demonstrations, making them a source of explicit adaptation.

The theoretical analysis focuses on linear transformers updated with a single gradient step. It characterizes how alignment between pretraining and the target task affects adaptation, explains how test-time training can alleviate distribution shift, and quantifies sample complexity. Within this setting, the analysis shows how adaptation can substantially reduce the number of examples eventually needed for in-context learning.

The empirical study applies test-time training to TabPFN, a foundation model for tabular data. The authors report that tabular classification requires three to five times fewer samples, with substantial inference-efficiency gains and negligible training cost. These findings align with the theory's account of sample savings, while the formal characterization itself remains specific to the analyzed linear-transformer update.
icml-2025-test-time-training-provably-im.tldr: Theory explains sample savings from test-time adaptation, and TabPFN experiments report three to five times fewer required classification samples.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to learn changing tasks without losing earlier knowledge. This paper studies why increasing model size has produced conflicting observations about forgetting. It separates scale from the degree of feature learning: lazy training changes representations relatively little, while rich training changes them more substantially.

Using a variable architecture parameterization, the authors find that increasing width helps when it reduces feature learning and makes training lazier. They then use dynamical mean field theory to analyze infinite-width dynamics in the feature-learning regime. This extends theoretical treatment of catastrophic forgetting beyond the lazy regime and connects forgetting to task non-stationarity.

In the study, high feature learning is beneficial only for highly similar tasks. Task similarity controls a transition from effectively lazy behavior with low forgetting to rich behavior with substantial forgetting. The authors also identify a critical feature-learning level that optimizes performance and transfers across model scales. The implication is that useful scaling depends on how representation changes match the degree of change between tasks.
icml-2025-the-importance-of-being-lazy-s.tldr: The study links continual-learning benefits from width to reduced feature learning and identifies task similarity as a key determinant of forgetting.

paragraphs: Lifelong model editing extends knowledge updates into a continuing sequence of edits. Methods developed for individual edits do not automatically maintain their performance in that setting. SimIE aims to connect the two areas, allowing standard parameter-modifying editors to benefit from a framework designed for repeated updates.

The method defines an ideal parameter change as the minimum-norm solution of a linear system, using the Moore-Penrose inverse. It derives recursive updates by truncating a limiting expression under two assumptions. This construction provides a mathematical target for sequential editing and a procedure for approximating that target as edits accumulate.

The analysis addresses failures of the assumptions: when either is unmet, the solution retains statistical near-optimality or stability against sequential-edit perturbations; when both fail, optimality and stability trade off. Experiments show that SimIE enables standard editing algorithms to perform comparably to specialized lifelong methods. The contribution offers both a practical bridge between editing settings and a conditional account of how its sequential updates behave.
icml-2025-towards-lifelong-model-editing.tldr: SimIE adapts standard model editors to repeated updates, achieving performance comparable to specialized lifelong methods with conditional theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Generating a time series often involves specifying structured attributes that describe the desired output. Such predefined fields may miss nuanced temporal behavior, and producing their labels can require expert effort. VerbalTS instead uses unstructured textual descriptions as conditions, aiming to make the requested characteristics more expressive and flexible.

The main technical problem is connecting descriptions in language with patterns in sequential data. VerbalTS introduces a multi-focal alignment and generation framework to model those relationships. Its objective encompasses both generating a time series and making the generated sequence correspond to the meaning of the text that conditions it.

Experiments on two synthetic and four real-world datasets show improvements over existing methods in generation quality and semantic alignment. These two findings address complementary requirements: the output should be a good time series and reflect the requested description. The work supports text as a useful interface for time-series synthesis in the evaluated settings, expanding the kinds of conditions available beyond predefined metadata fields.
icml-2025-verbalts-generating-time-serie.tldr: VerbalTS generates time series from free-form descriptions, improving generation quality and textual alignment across six evaluated datasets.
